stages.title: Demand-side policy trade-offs
stages.sub: After this you can explain the strength and weaknesses of demand-side policy and why growth and low inflation can conflict.

steps.q: The economy is in a slump with a negative output gap. The government cuts interest rates and raises spending, shifting AD to the right on the diagram. How quickly can this close the gap, compared to waiting for wages and prices to adjust on their own?
steps.right: Quite quickly, output can respond fast
steps.wrong: Only after several years of no policy change
steps.hint: Think about how fast a rate cut or spending boost feeds through into spending decisions, versus waiting for the whole economy to adjust by itself.

steps.right: No, conditions may have changed by then
steps.wrong: Yes, it reacts to the situation straight away

steps.q: A government uses stimulus to push unemployment down from 8% to 4%. As firms compete harder for scarcer workers and demand keeps rising, what tends to happen to inflation over that same period?
steps.hint: Lower unemployment usually comes from stronger demand. What does stronger demand do to prices?

steps.q: The government wants faster growth, which needs strong demand, but it also wants low, stable inflation, which needs demand not to run too hot. Can both be fully achieved with the same expansionary policy at once?
steps.right: No, pushing on growth risks higher inflation
steps.wrong: Yes, one setting satisfies both goals
steps.hint: Look back at the short-run trade-off between unemployment and inflation. Growth needs the same strong demand that also risks inflation.
